column7:
At the time of observation, the PK4 Tigers had recently returned from outdoor play and Library and were settled together on the carpet. Karen began by previewing the school day and involving students in familiar calendar routines. As she crossed out the days of the week using alternating colors, she asked students to identify which color should be used that day. When a student responded that orange was next, Karen prompted the student to explain the pattern, identifying that the colors followed a sequence of two black and two orange. She then reviewed the month of October and discussed November as the upcoming month, using the months displayed visually on the whiteboard to support the conversation. 

Karen transitioned students into a circle using a familiar Circle Song, reflecting well-established classroom routines. She then facilitated a greeting activity using a wooden tray. Students took turns knocking on the tray while classmates responded, Whos there? Each student then had an opportunity to creatively introduce themselves to the group, with Karen participating herself once all students had taken a turn. 

Karen followed this with an imaginative sharing activity. She began by pretending to give the student beside her a balloon. Each child then imagined an object they thought the next classmate might enjoy and passed it along - for example, one student offered an imaginary piece of Lego. When students needed additional language support, Karen provided a sentence stem so they could participate successfully. When a few students became silly during the activity, Karen paused the group, calmly reinforced the expectations for sharing, and referred students back to the visual expectations posted on the whiteboard before continuing.
column9: To what extent are the  learning experiences personalized to meet student's individual needs and interests?
column10: You provided multiple supports that allowed students with different linguistic and developmental needs to participate successfully in the group experience. In particular, offering a sentence stem when students struggled to express their imaginary gift gave them an accessible entry point without removing the thinking or choice from the activity. The visual reminders on the whiteboard similarly supported students in understanding the expectations independently.
column12: To what extent does collaborative learning enhance student learning and promote social well-being?
column13: You used the circle routines to intentionally strengthen relationships among the children. The imaginary-gift activity went beyond simply taking turns: students had to consider another child and think about something that person might enjoy. This invited early perspective-taking while also giving every child an opportunity to contribute to the group. Your decision to pause and revisit the shared expectations when the activity became silly also protected the conditions needed for respectful participation.
column14: What was your intention in asking each student to choose an imaginary object they thought the next child would like? I wonder how you might build on this by occasionally inviting the giver to explain why they selected that particular object, and the recipient to respond.
column16: How might we ensure students have opportunities to learn from each other's cultural backgrounds and experiences?
column18:
This is a game we played all week for our morning meeting. It was chosen to encourage conversation between two people. We sit randomly on the carpet for circle time so the individual might not be sitting next to a friend. We also have some students who are in the early stages of English acquisition. Repeating a set pattern of dialogue can help them become more confident in speaking English. By having the students choose an item they would like to gift to another child they might be inspired to think of what the other child likes and gain some perspective. It may show what they themselves are interested in. By playing this game all week, I am able to gain some information about whether or not a student has the ability to think of their friends interests.
I hope to repeat this game throughout the year with extensions such as the one you suggested (explaining why the giver chose this item) or having the recipient describe what they might do with the object (Thank you for the cupcake. I will eat it at snack time.). These extensions can stimulate thinking and making connections.

column7:
At the time of observation, Lovina and the 1A students began their mathematics lesson with a Math Talk. Lovina displayed an image of a farm scene containing several types of animals in different enclosures and provided students with one minute of quiet thinking time to consider what they noticed and wondered. During this time, she encouraged students to view the image through a mathematical lens and set a timer so all students had protected time to think before anyone responded. 

When the minute ended, students readily shared their observations and questions. Some responses were immediately mathematical, while others focused more generally on features of the image. Lovina consistently invited students to consider how their ideas might be expressed mathematically, supporting them in developing mathematical expressions that she then recorded on the screen. Students appeared familiar and confident with the Notice and Wonder routine and with the expectation that they would look for mathematics within an image or context. 

Lovina then transitioned the class into math centers. Four centers had been prepared in advance, and she clearly communicated where each student would begin. Lovina facilitated one center while the classroom Educational Assistant supported another.
column9: In what ways do students have opportunities to engage with their community through their learning projects?
column10: You intentionally protected one minute of individual thinking time before inviting responses, which ensured that every student first had an opportunity to develop an idea of their own. Students then willingly contributed their notices and wonderings rather than simply responding to a predetermined mathematical question. Their familiarity with the routine suggests they are developing confidence in seeing themselves as mathematicians whose ideas can contribute to the direction of the discussion.
column12: In what ways does the learning environment support risk-taking?
column13: You used the open-ended farm image to create space for students to see different mathematical possibilities within the same context. Rather than directing students toward one predetermined observation, you accepted a range of initial ideas and then prompted students to reconsider them mathematically. This helped students move from simply describing what they saw toward generating mathematical relationships and expressions from their own observations.
column14: How might students be invited to build on, question, or represent one anothers mathematical ideas during the Math Talk, so the discussion becomes more student-to-student rather than primarily student-to-teacher?
column16: How might we ensure students have opportunities to learn from each other's cultural backgrounds and experiences?
column18: In math, we are currently practicing using math talk signals to share our thinking. We have not yet started practicing accountable talk to add on to others' thinking, as students are still working on self-regulation. My goal is for students to be able to listen carefully to others' ideas and ask questions or build on that learning. To help with this, I am using different images at times to connect with class interests and encourage more student participation. The math talk we used today was not from IM, as IM talks are often not open-ended. IM primarily focuses on factual mental math expressions, which has led students to focus only on answers and move quickly to the next question. For example: ___ + 2 = 7 or 9 - ___ = 4.

column7:
Students began the observation seated at their tables participating in a mindful drawing activity. Naomi used a video tutorial to guide students through drawing a hammerhead shark and participated in the drawing alongside the students. When the artist in the video instructed students to draw three lines for the sharks gills, Naomi paused to ask students if they knew the purpose of gills. Several students called out a response, which Naomi repeated for the class. Students were then given five minutes to color their sharks. During this time, Naomi moved among the tables and interacted with students as they worked.

At the end of the five minutes, Naomi used the cue, Hands on top, and students responded, That means stop. She asked students to write their names on their papers and give them to Ms. Hannah, explaining that unfinished coloring could be completed later. Naomi verbally recognized one student for putting his name on his paper right away. Students were then asked to transition to the carpet. During the transition, Naomi wrote Nouns and Verbs on the board.

At the carpet, Naomi reminded students what nouns are and invited them to provide examples. All students except one raised their hands to contribute. Students initially provided several examples of places, and Naomi prompted them to think of things and people as additional examples. Naomi then reminded students that verbs are actions and asked them to share examples. Several students began combining actions with animals that could perform those actions.

Naomi introduced the next task by telling students that they would make a book. She asked students to recall whether the paper should be folded the hot dog way or hamburger way and which side of the book should be stapled. She explained that each student would receive two pieces of paper. After receiving their paper, students stapled their books with support from Ms. Hannah and returned to the carpet. During this process, Amelia brought her book to the observer to show it. When asked what she would put in her book, Amelia responded that she did not know. Naomi also told another student who asked about the task that she would explain what the book would be about once everyone returned to the carpet.

Once students returned, Naomi showed them her own book and explained that they could choose either a person or an animal as the subject. Students indicated with a thumbs-up when they had made their choice, and Naomi called on each student to share whether they had selected a person or an animal. Naomi explained that students would draw their selected person or animal on the front cover. When a student said they did not know how to draw their choice, Naomi responded that they could try their best. Naomi modeled the process by drawing Ms. Hannah on the cover of her book. She then explained that on the second page, students would draw their person or animal doing something. Naomi invited students to help generate an idea for an action Ms. Hannah could perform and modeled creating the next page showing an action.
column9: How might we ensure students are given voice and choice in the curriculum to reflect their cultural backgrounds and lived experiences?
column10: You regularly asked students to retrieve existing knowledge before introducing or extending ideas: the purpose of gills, examples of nouns and verbs, how to fold paper, and where to staple a book. This reflects a Tier 1 strategy of activating prior knowledge and aligns with UDL guidance to connect prior knowledge to new learning.
column12: What structures support students in practicing self-regulation or collaboration beyond the classroom?
column13: The hands on top/that means stop response, procedures for collecting drawings, transition to the carpet, and bookmaking routines provided explicit structures for students as they moved between activities. From an MTSS Tier 1 perspective, predictable routines and explicit directions provide universal supports that can reduce barriers to participation.
column14:
What might change if students knew the purpose and end product of the bookmaking task before gathering and stapling their materials? Could previewing the goal help students make more intentional choices while also supporting learners who benefit from knowing what is coming next? UDL specifically emphasizes clarifying the meaning and purpose of goals and organizing information and resources.

I'm also curious to know if you feel it might be a better use of time to just have the books already put together so students can focus on the writing part?
column16: In what ways are students empowered to make decisions about their learning?
column18:
Thank you for coming into my lesson and sharing your feedback. Upon reflection, I realised that I didnt explain the goal of the task clearly to students before they gathered and stapled their papers. Previewing the purpose and finished product could have helped students make more intentional choices and supported those who benefit from knowing what to expect. During individual work time, I did go around and help the students with their book writing and the understood that the learning goal was to make a book and to write a simple who/what and do sentence.

This was our second lesson on how to make a book, and I wanted students to revisit and reinforce the steps before moving towards using completed books made by me or making one more independently. During my next writing lesson, I would explain the goal and show an example first, then give students the opportunity to practise the bookmaking steps.

column7:
Students were seated at tables working on books about their holiday. Directions displayed on the board asked students to identify who was in their sentence and what they did. Several students shared their stories during the observation. Some books included sticky notes on which a teacher had written the words of the students story.

Kenya called for students attention and asked them to clean up and put their writing away in preparation for math. Students placed their writing in folders and returned the folders to the writing basket. During the transition, Kenya identified kind words exchanged between students and added a star to the class caring chart. She used this moment to ask students to think about the number of stars they had earned, including what comes after 10 and how many more stars they would need to reach 20.

Kenya introduced the math lesson by telling students they were learning about numbers and images. She read a story problem that was also displayed on the board and asked students what the story was about. When a student responded that it was about Diego, Kenya clarified that Diego was who the story was about. She reminded students to raise their hands rather than call out and then invited students with raised hands to respond. Students were asked to find a partner and think about ways they could act out the story. As students worked, Kenya supported one group by asking what they could do and what they might need to act out the story. When a student asked how many people were needed, Kenya referred the student back to the displayed story, and the student went to the visual and counted the people shown.

Kenya brought the class back together and asked students to share how they might act out the story. When a student suggested getting fruit, Kenya asked another student to collect six pieces of fruit to represent the six apples in the story. Another student identified that children were also needed. Students then acted out the story before returning to the carpet. Kenya asked what number is one more than five and asked students to explain how they knew. When some students began sharing other number combinations, Kenya redirected their attention to the question displayed on the board.

Kenya then explained that students would determine how many objects were in groups and circle the group that had more. She displayed a problem, worked through it with the class, and explained that students would complete similar work independently at their seats. She distributed the papers, which began with the same problem students had just completed together as a class.
column9: In what ways are students asked to take on an authentic societal role as part of their learning?
column10: You frequently responded to students with questions rather than immediately providing answers. For example, when a student wondered how many people were needed, you directed the student back to the visual to determine the answer. This provided an opportunity for the student to use an available resource to solve the problem.
column12: To what extent does collaborative learning enhance student learning and promote social well-being?
column13: You publicly noticed kind language during the transition and connected it to the class caring chart. This reinforced a classroom routine centered on how students interact with one another. UDL similarly identifies fostering belonging and community, developing awareness of self and others, and cultivating empathy as important aspects of engagement.
column14: The class moved from a shared example to the same starting problem on the independent worksheet. How might you use observations during partner and whole-group work to identify students who are ready to move ahead and those who need additional support, such as manipulatives, visuals, or teacher guidance, as part of Tier 1 instruction?
column16: How might assessment models be adapted to accommodate students from different linguistic and cultural backgrounds?
column18: After observation, if I realize that students need support or a challenge, I would have students begin the worksheet independently, then circulate and ask how they know which group has more. I would keep counters on the tables at all times for students who need support and pull a small group to model matching and counting one to one. I would keep challenge materials, larger groups, a how many more? question, or a make your own problem task, in a set spot so students who finish early and need a challenge know where to go. These are flexible Tier 1 supports; the learning goal stays the same for everyone, and I would adjust the next lesson based on what I saw.

column7:
- Grade 7 I&S class
- Start of observation: 10:25
- Approx. 20 students in the room (12 girls, 8 boys)
- Teacher is introducing a new unit. As students walked in, the teacher introduced the Statement of Inquiry for this unit and highlighted the key concepts. Good way to introduce a new unit to MYP students. This unit is about natural disasters and the main inquiry is about why natural disasters are more impactful to some communities than others. 
- Teacher is explaining certain key vocabulary and concepts that are central in this unit (e.g. natural hazard and natural disaster). Students are required to copy these definitions into their notebooks. 
- All the students have received a list of key vocabulary (in English), with Korean and Chinese translations and definitions. This is a very helpful tool for students to use during this unit. This list was created by the EAL support teacher that works with this class. 
- Next, the teacher provides the table group with a T-chart. Students are given a range of examples (e.g. a tsunami floods a coastal town). Students are required to identify if these examples are either a natural hazard or a natural disaster. Students should cut the examples and then glue it in their notebooks. They are allowed to collaborate during this activity. 
- The EAL support available in this class takes this opportunity to check in with certain students that need additional language support. 
- During the activity, the teacher is roaming around and asking clarifying questions. 'Why do you think this is a hazard and not a disaster?' This requires students to explain their reasoning and use their Thinking ATL skills.
column9: To what extent are the  learning experiences personalized to meet student's individual needs and interests?
column10: The learning experience included strong language scaffolds. The vocabulary list with Chinese and Korean translations, combined with targeted EAL support, gave multilingual learners multiple ways to access the key concepts of the new unit.
column13: The table-group sorting activity encouraged students to discuss whether examples were hazards or disasters, while teacher questioning such as Why do you think this is a hazard? pushed students to justify their reasoning and use Thinking ATL skills.
column14:
I am curious if it would have been a good idea to start this unit with some footage or news articles about some recent natural hazards or disasters (e.g. the mudslides in Nepal and China). I think this would have added some relevant context to this unit. 

Just a wondering from my end.

Thanks, Tim. Appreciate observing your class!

column7:
- Grade 8 Chinese L&L class
- Start of observation: 10:45
- 5 students in class (2 boys, 3 girls)
- At the start of the observation, students are, with the help of the teacher, analysing a piece of text about Leo Tolstoj, the famous Russian author. 
- The room displays the ATL posters (in Chinese), some student work, and vocabulary words in Chinese.
- Next, the students are provided with examplar posters (sort of graphic organisers) created by the other class that serves as an example for the graphic organisers the students need to make. 
- The teacher provides the students with a short brain break in the middle of class that will allow them to socialise, visit the washroom, etc.
- After the brain break, the teacher shows some examples of graphic organisers on the board to provide students with some inspiration and examples, after which they start this task.
column9: To what extent are the  learning experiences personalized to meet student's individual needs and interests?
column10:
Students were supported with clear visual models and examples before beginning the graphic organiser task.

The exemplar posters from another class and examples shown on the board gave students concrete reference points, making the expectations easier to understand and access.
column13:
Students had the opportunity to transform their understanding of the text into a visual graphic organiser.

Rather than only analysing the text verbally, students could represent their understanding in a more creative and visual format.
column14: How might students be given more choice over the format, structure, or visual style of their graphic organiser so they can decide how best to communicate their understanding?
column18: This is the last part of this unit. Because we were short on time before the holiday, I left this part until after the break. I was in a rush to finish the unit, so I just gave students some examples. It did support students in doing the task, but it also limited their creativity. I might have students brainstorm some ideas: What would you do if you wanted to clearly demonstrate the structure of a text? Based on students ideas, I could introduce several options. Maybe a graphic organizer is one of the ways to see how the author structures their content.

column7:
During the observation, students were seated on the carpet at the front of the classroom, using their iPads to participate in a Kahoot game. Students worked independently to answer questions presented in Chinese characters, selecting responses that were also written in Chinese characters. The game encouraged students to answer questions quickly. At the conclusion of each round, a student was identified as the winner. Following one round, many students stood up, talked loudly, and showed their screens as they moved into the next part of the game. One student remained seated at the side of the classroom throughout the activity. Students completed three rounds of the game, after which rankings were displayed on the board, identifying students in first, second, and third place across three different categories.

Following these rounds, Angelina asked students to put down their iPads and facilitated a brief discussion about how well they had worked together and how their answering speed had increased. Angelina then opened another round of Kahoot, allowing the class to choose which game they wanted to play. Before students began, she reminded them to read the questions carefully rather than rushing to answer. As students played, Angelina circulated around the classroom, observing their responses. Following the question-and-answer portion, students transitioned into another part of the game, during which several students began shouting and speaking loudly. Angelina reminded students to use quieter voices. When this portion of the game occurred again, students once more raised their voices while participating.
column9: To what extent does collaborative learning enhance student learning and promote social well-being?
column10: The use of Kahoot incorporated elements of play, technology, and immediate feedback into Chinese language practice. This aligns with the UDL principle of providing multiple means of engagement, particularly nurturing joy and play. Students participated in repeated rounds of practice with Chinese characters, providing opportunities to revisit and apply their language knowledge.
column12: How might we ensure students have opportunities to reflect on their planning, thinking, work, and/or progress?
column13: You reminded students to slow down and read questions carefully rather than rushing to answer. This encouraged students to focus on their thinking and accuracy, supporting the development of more intentional learning habits and self-monitoring strategies.
column14: How might the information gathered through Kahoot responses be used to identify students who need additional support with recognizing and reading Chinese characters, as well as students who are ready for greater challenges?
column16: How might assessment models be adapted to accommodate students from different linguistic and cultural backgrounds?
column18:
Thank you for visiting the Grade 4 Chinese A class. Students participated in the Kahoot activities to review what they learned from the mentor text (a narrative story), including vocabulary and reading comprehension. 

Using the data collected from Kahoot responses along with class observations and assessments, I can design and modify activities for students needing additional support with reading and recognizing Chinese characters, such as running small-group review with flashcards or character-component work; using pinyin-supported reading, and give shorter, more frequent practice sets. For students who are ready for greater challenges, I can facilitate them to independently analyze other narrative stories using strategies that they learned from understanding the mentor text. For example, summarizing main ideas, identifying character traits, applying new vocabulary in different contexts..

A note on the Submarine Kahoot game: To accomplish each level of challenge, one or two students were randomly selected by Kahoots system to announce and show the images on their iPads to the whole class, so that their classmates can quickly tab on the matching images. Students were allowed to shout out answers due to the structure of this game. But I will keep reminding them to speak at an appropriate voice level.

column7:
Vicki greeted students at the classroom door while playing her ukulele and singing the Criss Cross Applesauce song. Students entered the classroom singing along, and took their places on the carpet. Vicki reminded students of the Grizzly Bear song they had learned during their previous lesson. She began singing, and many students joined in. Vicki asked students if they remembered the game associated with the song and whether they could help sing it, with many responding yes to both questions. She sang the song again with the students, pausing at specific points to encourage stronger vocal participation.

Vicki then directed students to move to the circle carpet, where she led them in singing the song while walking in a circle. She invited one student to go to the middle of the circle and act as the bear. During this round, students had some difficulty maintaining the circle formation and moved closer to the student playing the bear. At the end of the round, Vicki supported the student in the middle in selecting another student to take on the role of the bear. The game continued through several rounds, with students taking turns in the center. During the third and fourth rounds, two students briefly stepped away from the circle. On both occasions, Ms. Kenix redirected them, and they quickly rejoined the activity. When one student expressed disappointment about not being chosen as the bear, Vicki gently encouraged her to continue singing so that she might be selected in a future round. The student responded by rejoining the game. As the activity continued, boys frequently selected other boys to take the next turn. Vicki and Kenix supported students in choosing classmates who had not yet participated as the bear. Toward the end of the game, Vicki suggested selecting two bears at a time so that the remaining students could have an opportunity to participate.

After all students had taken a turn as the bear, Vicki asked them to sit back down in a circle and introduced a new learning center. She explained that she would demonstrate how to use a new material, describing it as something special and exciting. Students responded with enthusiastic and increasingly loud vocalizations. Kenix reminded them to use calm bodies and quiet voices. Vicki reinforced expectations by explaining that, during the demonstration, students should keep their hands behind their backs and use their eyes to watch. She then led the group to the demonstration table to introduce the new material.
column9: To what extent does collaborative learning enhance student learning and promote social well-being?
column10: The game provided opportunities for students to take on a central role and make decisions by choosing the next bear. You monitored participation and supported students in including classmates who had not yet been selected. Adjusting the game to allow two bears at a time ensured that every student had an opportunity to participate. These practices connect to the Transformative Learning Goals of Agency and Collaboration by creating opportunities for student decision-making, peer interaction, and inclusion within a shared learning experience.
column12: How are adults modeling respectful, autonomy-supportive behavior?
column13: You and Kenix both used verbal reminders, redirection, and encouragement to support students' participation and self-regulation. These interactions reflect proactive Tier 1 practices that support participation, emotional regulation, and positive peer experiences.
column14: Students were given opportunities to choose the next bear, although they frequently selected peers of the same gender. What additional structures might support students in considering different classmates and ensuring equitable participation? How might students take greater ownership of managing turns and making inclusive decisions without relying on adult guidance ~ in an age-appropriate way?
column16: How might we ensure students have opportunities to learn from each other's cultural backgrounds and experiences?
column18: I noticed that this class didn't seem very familiar with the concept of choosing someone to go next. They also seemed to not know each other's names. I think playing more turn-taking games and name games will help them familiarize with each other. We have played some circle games where the next person is chosen based on when the song ends, and now I realize that hasn't required them to make a choice on their own. I think deliberately choosing games where they have to choose themselves will help them build this skill.

column7:
Students began the lesson seated on the carpet as Maria asked them to demonstrate different ways to represent a number using their hands. She prompted students to recall the representations they had explored the previous day, including hands, shapes, ten frames, dice, and tally marks. Maria then turned on the interactive board and invited volunteers to demonstrate how to represent the number five using tally marks. When one student represented seven using tally marks, Maria reminded the student to leave a space between the group of five and the additional two marks. Maria explained that students would be completing an assessment to demonstrate what they remembered from their learning. Assessment papers had been placed at different tables around the classroom, and students moved to a table to begin working. Maria reminded students to write their names on their papers before beginning.

Maria displayed the first assessment question on the interactive board, read it aloud with the students, and asked them to follow along. She circled the first question in purple, explained the task, and directed students to draw the towers and write the corresponding numbers. As students worked independently, Maria and Kacey circulated around the classroom to monitor progress and provide support. Maria asked students to give a thumbs-up when they were ready to continue. After a few minutes, most students had completed the first question, and Maria asked whether they were ready to move on to question two. This question contained three parts. Maria read the first part aloud and used a pink pen to circle where students should record their answers. She then asked students to give a silent thumbs-up when they were ready to continue. Once all students indicated they were ready, Maria read the second part and demonstrated how to answer the question. Throughout the assessment, Maria continued guiding students through the questions while Kacey circulated to support students who needed additional assistance.
column9: To what extent are the  learning experiences personalized to meet student's individual needs and interests?
column10: You used several strategies to support students in accessing the assessment, including reading questions aloud, displaying them on the interactive board, highlighting specific sections using different colors, and breaking multipart questions into smaller steps. These strategies reflect UDL principles of multiple means of representation and graduated support. The additional support provided by Kacey also created opportunities for students to receive assistance as they worked through the assessment.
column12: How are adults modeling respectful, autonomy-supportive behavior?
column13: You incorporated thumbs-up signals throughout the assessment to check students' readiness before moving forward. These nonverbal responses provided opportunities for all students to communicate their readiness without speaking aloud. This reflects Tier 1 strategies for checking student progress and maintaining participation during whole-group instruction.
column14:
How will the information gathered from this assessment be used to identify patterns in student understanding and plan next steps? Are there opportunities to use the results to create flexible groups, provide targeted practice with specific number representations, or extend learning for students who have already demonstrated understanding? 

I'm also curious to know how you are finding the assessments in the IM resource and what adjustments you might be thinking are needed for our context.
column16: How might assessment models be adapted to accommodate students from different linguistic and cultural backgrounds?
column18:
The assessment data is helping us identify patterns in student understanding, while also raising some important questions for us as a team about how we are using the IM assessments. We are finding that the section assessments and checkpoints often give us more useful information than the end-of-unit assessment because they help us identify specific skills, misconceptions, and areas that need further attention. This information is already helping us create flexible groups, revisit concepts with students who need more support, and provide additional challenge for students who have already demonstrated a strong understanding of the concept.
The end-of-unit assessment is still useful because it gives us an opportunity to look across the learning and identify concepts that may need to be revisited. We see mathematics as continuous learning, so these assessments are not an endpoint, but one source of evidence that helps us decide what students need next. At the same time, the amount of assessment can feel quite heavy, particularly when some tasks require individual support and take significant time away from instruction.
We are also noticing that strong assessment results do not always match what we see during independent activities. Some students can perform well on a structured assessment but may not yet demonstrate the same understanding independently, while others find parts of the curriculum too easy and begin to lose engagement. This is encouraging us to look at assessment results alongside classroom observations, student work, and performance during centers and problem-solving tasks.

column7:
Students were seated in groups at three tables with their math notebooks, working on an activity focused on comparing numbers to identify which number was less. Tammy called students to attention and reviewed the procedures for the game. Students were instructed to roll two markers on a number sheet, record the two numbers on their activity page, and circle the number that was less. Some students at one table were still unclear about the directions, so Maria and Jasmine walked them through the activity and supported them in working with their partners. Tammy checked in with one pair of students, asking whether they were helping each other determine which number was less. As students finished, Jasmine prompted them to check their answers with their partners. When asked how she knew that 1 was less than 6, one student demonstrated her thinking using her fingers.

Tammy brought the students back to attention and acknowledged their conversations with classmates about their mathematical thinking. She directed students to put their notebooks away and return to the carpet. Students placed their notebooks in their boxes and transitioned to the carpet. Tammy reviewed the activity and asked students to identify another word for "less," with students sharing "fewer." She then displayed the numbers 9 and 2 and asked students to identify which number was less and explain how they knew. One student used her fingers to demonstrate that 2 was less than 9.

Tammy then introduced the next task, explaining that students would complete a check for understanding before taking their test. She reminded students of the different ways they had learned to represent numbers and connected the task to the partner activity they had completed the previous day. She explained that students would now complete the task independently, choosing any number from 1 to 10 and showing that number in four different ways. Tammy asked Jasmine to explain the instructions in Chinese and looked toward a specific student to check his understanding. Before students began, Tammy asked them to restate what they were expected to do with their papers.
column9: To what extent does collaborative learning enhance student learning and promote social well-being?
column10: You provided students with opportunities to work with partners, compare answers, and explain their mathematical thinking. Your question about whether partners were helping one another, along with Jasmine's reminder to check answers together, reinforced the expectation that students support each other's learning. These practices connect to the Transformative Learning Goal of Collaboration and UDL's emphasis on fostering collaboration, interdependence, and collective learning.
column12: To what extent are the  learning experiences personalized to meet student's individual needs and interests?
column13: You reviewed procedures, modeled mathematical thinking through whole-group questioning, connected new work to previous learning, and asked students to restate directions before beginning. These practices reflect Tier 1 strategies of explicit instruction, scaffolding, and checking for understanding, and your use of students' explanations and representations also provided opportunities to gather formative assessment information.
column14:
The independent check for understanding asked students to represent a chosen number in four different ways. column18:

As a team, we are looking forward to each unit to see how we can take it slower and perhaps change the centers in order to do review. What we're finding is that it's hard to directly address what we're seeing in the checkpoints because we're moving to the next so in the next unit we want to look and see where we can slow down to add more review aspects. 

There is four assessments in some units and we are finding this quite a lot, we did decide to do them to reflect on how the kids were going but I don't know if it will be manageable going forward. We're just figuring it out as we go along and what works not only for our kids but for our time and planning.

column7: Observed Jake in Grade 3D during guided reading time. I observed him working with a group of three students on his EAL roster whose home languages are Korean and Chinese. They were going to read a book about weather. The students had notebooks with vocabulary words and meanings written down that they could reference or add more new words to. Two students were following instructions and responding to Jakes questions and prompts. One student seemed to be distracted but put her hand up, wanting to participate in reading aloud. Jake started the conversation by asking if they remembered the guest speaker from this morning. He used a whiteboard to write down words and their meanings for students to copy. The students needed a fair bit of prompting to understand who the guest speaker was and what they had spoken about. The guest speaker was a hurricane tracker. Jake prompted the meaning of both words, but students couldn't remember. One student was then able to compare a hurricane to a big storm like a typhoon. They then moved on to the words "predict" and "prediction" in connection to what a meterologist does. Jake had the students read two sentences with these words in them. He used some Korean to translate the parts of speech - predict is a verb (action), prediction is a noun. He also wrote them down on the whiteboard, asking the students to copy them into their noteboos. 2 students did this, 1 did not. Jake later let me know that these words are ones that have been on the board for the class to see and reference for a while but this group of students continue to struggle to retain the meaning.
column9: To what extent are the  learning experiences personalized to meet student's individual needs and interests?
column10: Jake, you provided several purposeful Tier 1 scaffolds to support your multilingual learners, including vocabulary notebooks, visual reinforcement through the whiteboard, repeated exposure to key words, and the use of Korean to clarify grammatical concepts. These strategies helped make the language of the text more accessible while providing students with resources they could revisit to support their understanding and independence.
column12: To what extent is student work authentic and reflective of that done by experts outside of school?
column13: I appreciated how you attempted to connect the guided reading text about weather to the students' experience with the hurricane trackers earlier that morning. Your questioning encouraged students to activate prior knowledge and make connections between new vocabulary and a real-world experience. It was encouraging to hear one student connect a hurricane to a typhoon, demonstrating an emerging understanding through a familiar concept. This also provided a valuable formative check of what students could recall and explain.
column14: You mentioned that students continue to find it challenging to retain the meanings of predict and prediction, despite repeated exposure. I wonder whether incorporating more multisensory and movement-based strategies might help strengthen retention. For example, students could create an action for predict (looking ahead or pointing to the future), physically demonstrate a prediction, or use gestures alongside oral sentences. Opportunities to act out, illustrate, explain, and apply vocabulary in different contexts could provide additional pathways for students to process and retrieve new language.

column18:
Hello, Sam. Thank you for visiting my class on Friday!

The girls are showing growth and are eager to learn and engage. Yu Chen tends to get shy when she is being observed, but I continue to see progress in all three students.

It was important for me to connect what we are learning in our unit with what the Hurricane Trackers shared with us that morning. I also wanted to see how much the girls understood and could recall from the presentation. We were able to make connections between that experience and our guided reading book, which is a grade-level text. I think it's important that students continue to engage with grade-level texts with appropriate scaffolds.

I appreciate your suggestion about using more movement and drawing to reinforce vocabulary. I will definitely try incorporating more of that. I think giving students more opportunities to demonstrate their understanding through movement, drawing, and speaking will help us see whether they are truly retaining these words. I also believe that repetition is kind, something I continue to emphasize with homeroom teachers. I include vocabulary in students' home languages on our slides, along with images when appropriate, so they have those resources to refer back to. During the lesson, I also explained the parts of speech in both Chinese and Korean to help make those connections clearer, as well as put the words into sentences that the students could more easily understand.

Thank you again for your feedback and suggestions!

column7:
Jessica co-teaching with Patti in 4A. 

On the TV is a large triangle divided into three sections.
"Cardiovascular System"
Jessica has been leading students through an inquiry. "What do you notice about how the words are grouped?"

Students identify that some words are in all of the body systems, others are just in the cardiovascular system. 
The learning focuses on identifying and categorising vocabulary within a nonfiction text about the human body.

Jessica is explaining the 3 different tiers - explaining the difference between everyday words, academic words and domain-specific vocabulary.

Jessica connects the discussion to the students' current UOI learning about body systems, using words such as arteries and cardiovascular as examples of vocabulary associated with a specific area of learning.

She refers to the vocabulary students encounter when reading nonfiction texts, including words highlighted in bold print. 

Jessica also connects this to writing, explaining that when writing about a particular body system, students need to use the specific vocabulary associated with that topic. "Reading like Writers".

Jessica refers to the cardiovascular system and asks students about their previous learning and modelling of the system.

Jessica hands over to Patti for the next part and Patti introduces the learning engagement and the the nonfiction mentor text the students have been using "Investigating the Human Body."

Students are asked to locate the text on EPIC and continue their learning about body systems. 
Patti refers to the previous day's work on the digestive system and explains that today they will look at the urinary system.

Students are asked to read the relevant section, identify vocabulary and categorise the words into the three tiers.
Students who finish the first section may continue identifying and categorising vocabulary from another section. (Endocrine System)

Patti checks that students understand where to find the text and what they need to record.

Students tranisition, collecti IPADs and their UOI books. Some students are listening to the text while others are finding their materials and preparing their pages. Some students use a translation app for scienctific vocabulary. 

Jessica and Patti move around the room to support students.
Jessica supports Anson as students settle into the activity. 
Patti also checks in with Anson as he begins his work.
Patti supports Jack. 
(Anson and Jack are lower level English  (MLL) )

Some students have drawn and labelled their vocabulary triangles with the labels  everyday, academic and domain-specific.

column7:
The Grade 12 Theory of Knowledge class included all DP candidates together in a shared classroom, with James and three other teachers co-teaching the course. Students were already seated in smaller groups when I entered, and James was leading a section of the lesson.
The session focused on the TOK essay, with the topic identified as Exploration in the TOK Essay. James was providing instructions about the next stage of the essay process.
Students were instructed to complete a form on ManageBac, selecting questions for the next stage of the process. James explained the task and directed students to the relevant form.
Students remained in their smaller groups while working on the task. Three teachers circulated among the groups, checking in with students and providing support.
column9: What structures support students in practicing self-regulation or collaboration beyond the classroom?
column10:
James, I really liked seeing the way you and the TOK team worked together to support students as they moved through the next stage of their essay process. Co-teaching a course with the entire Grade 12 DP cohort brings its own challenges, but I appreciated how you took the lead in providing clear instructions while your colleagues were available to work directly with students in their smaller groups. It was encouraging to see the teachers circulating, checking in with students and providing guidance as they considered their essay questions and next steps.
I also think the structure of the lesson provided a valuable opportunity for students to practise the self-management and collaborative skills they will need beyond the classroom. Having students work in smaller groups while taking responsibility for selecting their TOK essay questions gave them space to consider their own thinking, seek guidance and make decisions about their next steps. The ManageBac form also provided a clear structure for students to record those decisions and move forward with the process. I particularly appreciated how the collaborative approach of the teaching team supported this, with students having access to different teachers and their expertise while remaining responsible for their own essay development. This was a good example of how collaboration between teachers can create the conditions for greater student independence and self-regulation.
column12: In what ways are students empowered to make decisions about their learning?
column13: It was great the way students were being given responsibility for making decisions about the direction of their TOK essays. Rather than simply being directed towards a particular question, students were asked to consider the available prescribed titles and make their own selections through ManageBac. I particularly appreciated that this was happening within a structure where students could access guidance from the TOK teaching team as they worked through their thinking. The smaller groups and opportunities to check in with different teachers provided support without taking ownership of those decisions away from students. I think this is particularly important at this stage of the DP, where students need to develop the confidence to make informed academic decisions, evaluate their own ideas and take responsibility for the direction of their work. It was encouraging to see students being given that responsibility while still having access to the guidance and expertise of the teaching team.
column14:
James, thanks for having me in your class. I appreciated seeing students being given responsibility for selecting their TOK essay questions, with the support of the teaching team available as they considered their options. I wonder how you might build on this by encouraging students to take greater intellectual risks as they begin exploring their chosen questions. TOK provides such a valuable opportunity for students to challenge assumptions, consider unfamiliar perspectives and explore ideas that might initially feel uncomfortable or difficult to defend. There could be opportunities for students to share an initial interpretation of a question, test a less obvious argument with their peers, or explore a perspective that challenges their own thinking before committing to a particular direction. I think creating space for this kind of experimentation, where students feel comfortable questioning their ideas and changing their minds, could help them develop more thoughtful and nuanced arguments while building confidence in their own thinking.
How might you and the TOK team create opportunities for students to take intellectual risks, explore unfamiliar or challenging perspectives, and feel comfortable testing ideas that may not ultimately become part of their final essays?
column16: In what ways does the learning environment support risk-taking?
column18: Thank you for the feedback.  I agree that we should encourage our G12's to take intellectual risks and develop curiosity.  I believe the time together as a grade level gives us an opportunity to do so.  I think we could encourage the students to sit together in prescribed title groups and ask them to each develop arguments with example.  We could then ask students to evaluate arguments using the assessment criteria.

column7:
12 students were present and seated in pairs, working individually on their computers. Students were working on MYP Design Criterion C, specifically C2 and C3, as they moved from their design plans into creating their solutions.
Students were using Autodesk Fusion to develop their designs. One student was working on a detailed RAMS logo design, using dimensions and constraints within the software, while another student was developing the outline of a laser-cut design. Students also had planning documents open alongside their design work.
Nneka was positioned at the front of the classroom and asked students to bring their computers to her to discuss their work. Students approached Nneka individually with their devices and spoke with her about their progress.
The classroom display showed guidance for C2, Demonstrate Technical Skills, and C3, Follow the Plan to Create the Solution. The example included a step/date, actual time taken, a description of the process, materials, safety considerations and photographs documenting the work. For C3, students were prompted to identify whether they had followed their original plan and to describe and justify any changes they had made.
One student had a C1 planning document open that asked them to work from their initial ideas towards design development and create a plan for how they were going to make their product. The document included a table for recording steps in the process, resources/tools/materials, estimated time and quality-control considerations.
The classroom was very quiet throughout the observation, with students focused on their individual work and very little student-to-student conversation. Nneka continued meeting with students individually while the rest of the class worked independently.
column9: In what ways are students creating products or performances for authentic audiences?
column10:
Nneka, I really liked seeing students actively moving from their ideas and planning into the creation of an actual product. Students were using Fusion to develop their designs with the precision and technical detail needed for laser cutting, which gave the work a clear purpose beyond simply completing an academic task. I particularly liked that students were having to think about how their ideas would translate from something on a screen into a physical product that someone could actually use or engage with. The RAMS logo design was a nice example of this connection to an authentic school context and audience.
There were also some clear Tier 1 supports helping all students navigate what is quite a complex design process. The C2 and C3 example displayed at the front of the room made the expectations visible, including how students could document their technical process, use photographs as evidence, and explain changes from their original plan. Having that model available while students worked independently gave them a clear reference point without taking away their ownership of the individual products they were creating.
column12: To what extent do students have the opportunity to design, create, make, or otherwise add value that is unique to them?
column13:
The amount of space students had to make the design process their own was great. Although everyone was working through the same Criterion C requirements, the products I saw developing in Fusion were clearly individual, with students making their own decisions about shape, imagery, dimensions and how their ideas would translate into a finished product. It was particularly encouraging to see students working independently through quite different design challenges rather than following a single teacher-created model.
I also liked that the planning and documentation requirements provided enough structure to support students through the process without prescribing what the final outcome needed to look like. Students had a clear framework for planning, creating and documenting their work, while still having considerable freedom to make their own design decisions. This felt like a really nice balance between the structure students need and the creative freedom to produce something that is genuinely unique to them.
column14:
Nneka, thanks for having me in your class. I was really impressed by the level of focus and independence students demonstrated while working through their individual designs. At the same time, I was struck by just how quiet the room was. I recognise that students were working on their own individual products and were at different points in the design process, and I am sure there have been opportunities for discussion, feedback and collaboration in previous lessons. I wonder, though, how those opportunities might continue even during this more independent stage of the design process. Design naturally involves sharing ideas, troubleshooting, seeking feedback and learning from how others approach a problem, and there is real value in students seeing one another as resources alongside the individual support you were providing.
How might you maintain the strong individual focus I saw while continuing to create opportunities for students to talk, troubleshoot and learn from one another throughout the design process?

column7:
At the time of observation, the 2C students arrived in the gymnasium and immediately lined up in front of Joe. He began the lesson by asking students to complete three laps around the outside of the basketball court as a physical warm-up. Once finished, students independently seated themselves in four predetermined rows and settled quickly for instruction. 

Joe reviewed some of the technical rules of handball using diagrams on the whiteboard and invited students to contribute what they already knew about the game. He then revisited the four essential skillsdribbling, passing, shooting, and catchingreminding students that they had previously practiced dribbling and explaining that today's focus would introduce passing and catching. 

To teach the passing technique, Joe first physically modeled the movement step by step. When one student noticed that the motion resembled a pass in American football, Joe affirmed the connection and extended it to throwing in baseball and long passes in basketball. Joe then shifted some of the thinking to the students by asking them to direct his body through the correct passing motion. Students called out instructions while Joe followed their directions, allowing them to articulate their understanding of the technique. He then modeled catching with a student volunteer. When the student made a technical error, Joe used the moment to clarify the correct catching technique for the class. 

The opening physical warm-up and direct instruction lasted approximately ten minutes. Students then transitioned into a familiar dribbling activity before moving toward the new learning around passing and catching.
column9: How might personalized learning experiences foster a sense of community?
column10: You provided students with multiple entry points into understanding the skills of handball through diagrams, verbal explanation, physical demonstration, and opportunities to connect the movement to sports they already knew. When a student connected the passing motion to American football, you built on that prior knowledge by making additional connections to baseball and basketball. This helped make the new technique more accessible by linking it to existing experiences and presenting the learning in several modes.
column12: How might we elevate student voice in ways that build peer or adult respect?
column13: You created an effective moment of student ownership when you asked the class to direct your body through the handball passing motion rather than simply demonstrating it again yourself. Students became the ones articulating the sequence while you responded to their directions. This shifted them from watching the technique to actively communicating their understanding and briefly positioned students as the drivers of the instructional talk.
column14: What was your intention in how you responded to the technical error during the catching demonstration? I wonder whether there might also be opportunities for students to first notice what happened, identify what could be adjusted, and suggest a correction themselves.
column16: How might we ensure students have opportunities to reflect on their planning, thinking, work, and/or progress?
column18:
My intention was not particularly deliberate in that moment. I reacted quickly to clarify the technical error so that we could keep the lesson moving and give students more time to practice the skills. My focus was on ensuring that students understood the correct catching technique before moving on to the next activity.
However, looking back, I recognize that I could have used this moment as a more meaningful learning opportunity by asking students to observe what happened, identify the mistake, and suggest how the technique could be improved. This would have encouraged them to think more critically, take greater ownership of their learning, and develop a deeper undestanding of the correct catching technique.

column7:
Students were seated at tables and on the carpet with their readers notebooks open, taking notes while watching a video about blood and how it functions in the body. Kent acknowledged the work students were doing during the video, specifically highlighting their watching, thinking, listening, and note-taking. As students watched, Kent created sketchnotes on the board to capture information from the video.

Following the video, Kent asked students what they had noticed. One student shared his understanding of how blood works, and Kent built on his explanation by drawing a road on the board and using the analogy of a truck traveling along the road to illustrate how blood transports nutrients to different parts of the body. Kent asked students what other important information they had learned and introduced the abbreviations O2 (oxygen) and CO2 (carbon dioxide), connecting these terms to their understanding of how the body uses oxygen and produces carbon dioxide. Kent acknowledged the students' work and provided additional time for them to finish their notes.

Kent then directed students to put away their readers notebooks and prepare to transition to writing. Students put away their folders, some chatted with Kent, and others began returning to their tables. Kent acknowledged the class for their transition. Before beginning independent writing, Kent explained that he wanted to share some tips based on what he had noticed in students' published writing. He introduced the sentence structure of cause and effect, asking students to raise their hands if they had heard of it before. A few students raised their hands. When Kent asked for an explanation, he called on the same student who had shared his understanding during the earlier discussion about blood.

Kent provided examples of cause-and-effect sentences, highlighting the connecting words because, since, and so. As he read example sentences, he asked students to identify the words that indicated cause and effect. He then challenged students to incorporate at least one cause-and-effect sentence into their own writing.
During the independent writing period, students were working on list articles. Students at one table explained that they could choose to write about anything they knew how to do. One student shared (with me) her writing template and the notes she had used to generate possible topics for her article. Kent stepped out of the classroom to observe another teacher, while Snow remained to support students during their independent writing time. During the approximately five to seven minutes following the start of independent work, several students took a lot of time to begin writing. At the table being observed, students spent the majority of the time looking at their papers, and each student wrote approximately one sentence during that period. This was noted at many tables around the room with the exception of the one table where Snow was supporting.

column10: You incorporated multiple approaches to presenting and reinforcing information during the science video, including visual sketchnotes, student discussion, vocabulary clarification, and the analogy of trucks transporting nutrients along a road. These approaches reflect Tier 1 instructional strategies that provide multiple entry points for students to access grade-level content.

column7:
During the lesson, students were seated at tables with copies of an exemplar letter and were asked to read like writers. Audrey began by reminding students of an example of an opening sentence that had made them feel an emotion. She then read the first paragraph of the exemplar letter aloud and asked students to identify what the author had done as a writer. Students noted that the author had stated a clear opinion. Audrey also drew attention to how the writer had named a specific space that the reader could visualize. When a student commented that this made the writing more specific, Audrey acknowledged the observation. Audrey continued by reading the second paragraph and asking students to discuss with a partner why the writer had included survey information. As students talked, Audrey checked in with several partnerships. She then shared observations from the discussions with the class and explained that facts can be more persuasive than opinions.

As Audrey moved into the next paragraph, she paused to ask students about the meaning of the word communal. After reading the third paragraph, she asked students to discuss with their partners why the writer had included such specific information. Audrey circulated and checked in with two groups during these conversations. She then shared with the class that she had heard reflections and feedback being exchanged between partners. 

Audrey asked students to put down their pencils and highlighters and guided them through checking whether they had identified all the important parts of the letter. During this process, most students referred to their copies of the letter, using a different colored highlighter or pencil to check their work. Audrey continued reading the next section of the letter and asked students to notice the emotion communicated by the writer. She also asked students to explain the meaning of humidity and consider how humidity makes people feel.

You encouraged students to think about why the author made certain writing choices and how those choices affect the reader. This connects our Transformative Learning Goal of Authenticity by helping students understand how writers use language and evidence to communicate with an audience.
